strengths: Significance: Adaptive, variable-length tokenization addresses a useful efficiency problem in autoregressive time-series forecasting. Table 4 and the compression visualizations demonstrate that the tokenizer adapts substantially across datasets and temporal patterns.

Soundness: BPE merges preserve the quantized sequence exactly, and Equation (6) correctly gives the empirical squared-error-minimizing reconstruction for each observed symbol pair. These components are simple and technically understandable.

Originality: Applying motif-based BPE to a forecasting foundation model is a useful integration. The investigations of quantization granularity, motif frequency, tokenizer training-set size, and learned embeddings provide additional empirical insight.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable, with helpful diagrams, pseudocode, vocabulary statistics, and compute estimates. Evaluating three tokenizers and five model sizes provides meaningful evidence of practical accuracy–latency tradeoffs.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Section 5.3 and Appendix C.3 state that model-dependent conditional decoding is fitted to model predictions on each target dataset's training split. Consequently, the Ours_cd results in Tables 2–3 involve supervised target-domain adaptation, despite being presented as zero-shot comparisons against unadapted baselines. This is not test-set leakage, but it materially changes the evaluation setting. The Chronos-trained, model-independent decoder in Table 10 does not establish the same headline gains.

Soundness—attribution to motifs: Matching 128 input tokens gives Chronos 128 raw observations but gives the proposed method a substantially longer, data-dependent history. Matching training tokens also exposes the methods to different numbers of raw observations. These are legitimate compute-budget comparisons, but they do not isolate motif quality. Matched raw-context experiments and a sample-wise baseline using the same coarse quantization and normalization are needed to distinguish BPE's contribution from longer context and quantization-induced smoothing.

Soundness—headline efficiency: Table 2 combines the best MSE and fastest qualifying model from separate selections over tokenizer and model size. The reported 36.1% accuracy improvement and 19.90× acceleration therefore do not describe one configuration achieving both. Much of the acceleration can also reflect model downsizing; Appendix C.4 reports generation compression of only approximately 1.4–2.1×. Report the selected configurations and paired accuracy/latency, alongside same-size comparisons and end-to-end timing including tokenization. The 0.26× Weather result also shows that acceleration is not consistent.

Evaluation validity: Appendix C.2 compares this method's 64-step forecasts with published baselines forecasting 96 steps from 192 observations. The resulting '19 out of 25' claim is not supported by a common forecasting task. Tables 2–3 also select the best models using reported test results without describing an independent selection procedure. Patch-based comparisons vary architecture, training data, and training objective, as the paper acknowledges, so they cannot establish that adaptive tokenization itself is superior.

Reproducibility: Appendix B largely refers readers to Chronos hyperparameters and says evaluation is performed once. Important details remain unspecified: normalization statistics and their temporal scope, sampling and point-forecast aggregation, variable-length generation stopping and truncation, treatment of unseen conditional-decoding pairs, and the latency measurement protocol. There are no repeated-run uncertainty estimates. These omissions make the unusually poor Chronos results, particularly on Traffic, difficult to diagnose or reproduce.

Originality and interpretation: Both BPE and conditional-mean reconstruction are established techniques; the main novelty is their application and empirical behavior in this setting. Several stronger interpretations exceed the evidence: negative correlations between motif length and error in Table 6 do not demonstrate that longer motifs cause better forecasts, since smoother segments can be both easier to compress and easier to predict. Likewise, differing compression on ETTh1 and ETTm1 does not establish sampling-frequency invariance.

Limitations and ethics: No material ethical concern is apparent, and reporting compute expenditure is useful. However, the limitations discussion focuses mainly on absent hyperparameter tuning and alternative architectures. It should also delimit the single short forecast horizon, target-domain decoder fitting, out-of-range quantization behavior, and uncontrolled comparisons. Overall, the useful tokenizer idea merits further study, but unresolved evaluation issues prevent the central performance and generalization claims from supporting acceptance.

strengths: Originality and significance: Applying BPE to quantized time series is a useful adaptation that enables variable-length input and output tokens within standard autoregressive models. Compressing generated sequences, as well as contexts, offers a plausible practical benefit.

Soundness: The basic tokenizer is straightforward, and Equation (6) correctly gives the empirical squared-error minimizer for each observed symbol pair. Conditional decoding is simple and inexpensive for the proposed vocabulary sizes.

Evaluation: The paper explores five model sizes, three quantization settings, and five datasets, with additional ablations on motif frequency and vocabulary-training data size. The compression distributions and embedding analyses provide useful descriptive evidence.

Presentation and ethics: The method is generally well organized, with illustrative figures, pseudocode, and computational resource estimates. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described datasets and application.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Section 5.3 explicitly fits conditional decoding on model forecasts from each target dataset’s training split. This is target-specific supervised calibration, yet Tables 2–3 include these results under zero-shot forecasting. It is a legitimate evaluation setting, but it must be distinguished from zero-shot transfer and compared with similarly calibrated baselines. The source-trained, model-independent experiment in Appendix C.3 does not establish the same forecasting gains.

Soundness—insufficient isolation of tokenization effects: Section 4 fixes context length at 128 tokens, giving motif models substantially more raw historical observations than Chronos. Equal training tokens and gradient steps also do not imply equal exposure to raw time-series samples. These choices can demonstrate a useful fixed-token-budget advantage, but do not establish that motif representations themselves cause the accuracy improvement. Matched raw-context comparisons, a quantization-only baseline with identical bins and normalization, and a controlled fixed-patch baseline are needed.

Significance—headline efficiency gains require qualification: Table 2 separately selects the lowest-MSE model and the fastest model beating the Chronos reference. Thus, the reported 36.1% accuracy improvement and 19.90× acceleration are not a jointly achieved operating point. Speedups also include changing model size, and the 56.66× Traffic result uses a baseline the authors describe as diverging. The Weather result without conditional decoding is actually a slowdown at 0.26×. Report paired accuracy–latency results, same-size comparisons, and end-to-end timing details before attributing these gains to tokenization.

Soundness—baseline comparisons do not support several broad claims: The patch-based models differ in pretraining data, objectives, and architecture, as Section 5.2 acknowledges; their comparison cannot isolate adaptive tokenization. Table 3 also contradicts the statement that the method outperforms all MOMENT models: without conditional decoding, Weather MSE is 0.251 versus 0.240 for MOMENT-large. More seriously, Appendix C.2 compares the proposed 64-step forecasts with published baselines forecasting 96 steps from a different context length, undermining the claimed 19-of-25 advantage.

Reproducibility: Appendix B largely delegates training hyperparameters to Chronos and reports a single evaluation without uncertainty estimates. Important details remain unclear, including whether normalization uses only available history, forecast sampling and point-estimate construction, stopping and truncation for variable-length outputs, treatment of unseen symbol pairs in conditional decoding, and the latency measurement protocol. Selecting the best tokenizer/model on reported test results without a stated validation-selection procedure further weakens reliability.

Originality and interpretation: The technical ingredients are established BPE and conditional sample means; the contribution is primarily their adaptation and empirical validation. The broad 'first pattern-centric' claim needs stronger positioning relative to existing adaptive tokenization and token-merging work, including cited reference [1]. Moreover, the weak negative correlations between motif length and error in Table 6 do not show that longer motifs cause better forecasts: smoother, easier segments may both compress better and have lower error.

Scope and limitations: Five datasets at a single 64-step horizon provide limited support for broad foundation-model generalization claims. The limitations section acknowledges expensive hyperparameter tuning, but does not address target-specific calibration, comparison confounds, or behavior under clipping and distribution shift. These are material limits on the present evidence, rather than objections to the authors’ honest disclosure of limitations.

strengths: Originality: Applying BPE to quantized time series is a useful adaptation of an established technique. Variable-length motifs offer a practical alternative to sample-wise tokens and fixed patches, with interpretable vocabulary entries.

Soundness: The tokenizer construction is straightforward, and the conditional-mean decoder in Equation (6) correctly minimizes the stated empirical squared-error objective for observed symbol pairs. BPE compression introduces no additional reconstruction loss beyond quantization.

Significance: The experiments show promising accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across five datasets, three tokenizers, and five model sizes. Table 4 and the qualitative examples demonstrate substantial variation in compression across temporal patterns. The vocabulary-size and training-data ablations provide useful implementation insights.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable, with helpful diagrams, tokenizer pseudocode, explicit vocabulary settings, and computational-cost estimates. The authors acknowledge differences between pretrained baselines and disclose that conditional decoding uses target-dataset training splits. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Section 5.3 and Appendix C.3 fit the main conditional decoder on model predictions and targets from each evaluation dataset’s training split. This is supervised target-domain adaptation, although Tables 2–3 describe the resulting comparisons as zero-shot. Appendix C.3 separately studies a decoder trained on Chronos data, but primarily reports reconstruction-error reduction rather than establishing equivalent forecasting gains. The adapted and genuinely zero-shot results need separate labeling and matched baseline calibration.

Soundness—attribution to tokenization: Using 128 tokens for both methods gives motif models a longer and variable raw-time context than Chronos. Matching training tokens also does not match the amount of underlying time-series data processed. These are legitimate operational advantages, but they do not isolate the claimed benefit of motif structure. Matched-context comparisons and a quantization-matched baseline without BPE are needed to distinguish motif benefits from additional context, data exposure, and coarse-quantization effects.

Soundness and presentation—headline efficiency: Table 2 combines the best-MSE model and a separately selected fastest model outperforming Chronos. Thus, the advertised 36.1% accuracy gain and 19.90× acceleration are not demonstrated jointly by one configuration. Speedups also include changing model size, and the Weather result without conditional decoding is 0.26×, a slowdown. Report paired accuracy and latency for identified configurations, clarify validation-based selection, and distinguish tokenizer gains from model downsizing. The timing protocol does not adequately specify batching, sampling, synchronization, or whether tokenization and decoding are included.

Evaluation validity: Appendix C.2 compares the proposed 64-step forecasts against published baselines forecasting 96 steps from a different context length. Consequently, the claimed wins in 19 of 25 comparisons do not establish superiority under a common task. The patch-based comparisons also change architecture, pretraining data, and objectives; despite acknowledging this, Section 5.2 interprets them as evidence for adaptive tokenization. A controlled fixed-patch baseline is missing.

Reproducibility: Appendix B largely delegates training settings to Chronos and reports a single evaluation without uncertainty estimates. Important details remain unclear: normalization statistics and their temporal scope, generation and forecast aggregation, handling motifs that cross the prediction horizon, unseen symbol-pair fallback, and the exact selected checkpoints. The manuscript also needs an explicit pretraining/evaluation overlap audit to substantiate zero-shot generalization.

Originality and strength of interpretation: Conditional decoding is an empirical conditional-mean lookup; comparison against a learned per-symbol mean is necessary to establish the value of conditioning on the previous symbol. Its training-objective optimum does not guarantee forecasting improvements under distribution shift. Likewise, the weak negative correlations in Table 6 do not establish that longer motifs cause better forecasts: smoother, easier segments may both compress more and incur lower error.

Significance and limitations: The contribution is promising, but general claims about foundation-model forecasting rest on five datasets and one short forecast horizon, without probabilistic-quality evaluation. The limitations discussion focuses on untuned hyperparameters and alternative architectures while leaving the more consequential calibration, comparison, and evaluation restrictions insufficiently addressed. These evidential issues, rather than the method’s simplicity, prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality: Applying BPE to quantized time series provides a simple, useful mechanism for variable-length motif tokenization. Its integration with categorical forecasting and conditional reconstruction is a coherent contribution, even though the underlying components are established.

Soundness: BPE preserves the quantized sequence, and Equation (6) correctly gives the empirical squared-error-minimizing reconstruction for observed symbol pairs. Table 12 demonstrates meaningful accuracy improvements and roughly 1.4–2.3× inference speedups at matched model sizes.

Significance: Adaptive compression could benefit autoregressive forecasting. The analysis demonstrates substantial variation in input compression across datasets, and the quantization-only ablation in Table 13 provides evidence that motifs contribute beyond coarse discretization on several datasets.

Presentation and reproducibility: The method is generally understandable, with pseudocode, detailed result tables, training hyperparameters, hardware and computational costs. Six-seed experiments and ablations of vocabulary size, discretization, training-data size, and robustness strengthen the empirical investigation.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Section 5.3 fits conditional decoding on forecasts and labels from each target dataset's training split. This is supervised adaptation, yet Tables 2 and 3 describe the resulting comparisons as zero-shot. Baselines do not receive equivalent calibration. Appendix C.3 examines a genuinely dataset-independent decoder, but reports quantization-error recovery rather than comparable absolute forecasting results. The headline conditional-decoding gains therefore do not establish improved zero-shot forecasting.

Soundness—experimental isolation: Using 128 tokens for both Chronos and motif models gives the latter substantially more historical samples; equal training-token budgets also expose compressed models to more underlying samples. Patch models additionally use a different loss and 384 context samples. These are reasonable deployment choices, but they do not support the repeated claim that tokenization is the only experimental difference. Matched raw-context and data-exposure controls are needed.

Presentation of efficiency: The 19.90× headline averages speedups obtained by selecting smaller models that outperform a larger reference, whereas the reported 36.1% accuracy gain selects potentially different models. These are separate operating points, not a jointly achieved improvement. Table 12 supports much smaller matched-size speedups, and no corresponding runtime comparison against patch-based baselines establishes the claimed efficiency advantage over patching.

Evaluation validity: Table 11 compares this method's 64-step forecasts with published baselines forecasting 96 steps from different contexts, so the claimed 19-of-25 wins are not controlled comparisons. Section 5.2 also says the uncalibrated method beats all patch-based Chronos models except on ETTh1, but Table 3 contains better patch results on ETTm1 (0.608 versus 0.637) and Electricity (0.146 versus 0.150).

Reproducibility: Important details are unspecified, including forecast sampling and point-estimate aggregation, normalization statistics available at prediction time, inference batch size, treatment of unseen symbol pairs in conditional decoding, and model/tokenizer selection using validation data. The manuscript also does not document a pretraining-overlap audit for its zero-shot benchmarks or provide an implementation/checkpoint link.

Significance and limitations: Evaluation covers only five datasets and one 64-step horizon, leaving long-horizon and probabilistic forecasting benefits unestablished. Weak negative correlations between motif length and error do not demonstrate that longer motifs cause better forecasts, since easier segments may produce longer motifs. The limitations discussion mainly addresses absent hyperparameter tuning rather than these substantive constraints. No material research-ethics concern is apparent, but the evidential and comparison issues require resolution before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Adaptive tokenization addresses a useful efficiency problem in autoregressive forecasting. Quantization followed by BPE provides variable-length representations with an explicit reconstruction-error bound within the quantization range. Table 12 demonstrates real inference-time improvements at matched model sizes.

Originality: Applying a learned motif vocabulary to forecasting is a useful synthesis of symbolic time-series representations and BPE. The contribution also includes empirical understanding of vocabulary size, quantization granularity, compression, and learned embeddings.

Soundness: The conditional-mean estimator in Equation (6) correctly minimizes the stated empirical squared reconstruction error for observed symbol pairs. The appendix includes valuable controls, particularly discretization without motifs, robustness experiments, and six-seed evaluations for selected configurations.

Presentation and reproducibility: The method is generally understandable, with helpful illustrations, pseudocode, model hyperparameters, hardware specifications, and computational-cost estimates. The experiments cover five model sizes and several tokenizer configurations.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims mix incompatible evaluation settings. Section 5.3 fits conditional decoding to model forecasts and ground truth from each target dataset’s training split, yet Tables 2, 3, and 11 include these adapted results under zero-shot comparisons. This is legitimate supervised calibration, but it is not a wholly zero-shot pipeline and gives the method target-domain supervision unavailable to the comparison models. Appendix C.3 explores source-trained decoding, but does not establish the same headline forecasting gains under that protocol.

Soundness—the comparisons do not isolate tokenization as claimed. Section 4 gives both sample-wise Chronos and motif models 128 context tokens, corresponding to different amounts of historical data; equal training-token budgets similarly expose compressed models to more underlying samples. Patch models receive a fixed 384-sample context and use MSE instead of cross-entropy. These are reasonable practical configurations, but matched raw-context and training-data controls are needed to distinguish representation benefits from additional information and altered objectives.

Presentation and significance—the headline 19.90× acceleration and 36.1% MSE improvement summarize different selected operating points. Table 2 independently selects the best-MSE model and the fastest model exceeding the reference’s accuracy, often comparing different model sizes. For example, Table 12 shows approximately 1.9× acceleration for large models on ETTh1, whereas Table 2 reports 24.88× using a smaller model. The table explains the selection, but the abstract does not adequately qualify it. Weather’s uncalibrated accuracy-matching configuration is actually slower, at 0.26×.

Soundness—some claimed superiority is contradicted by the reported numbers. Section 5.2 says the tokenizer beats all patch-based Chronos models except on ETTh1, but without conditional decoding it also loses to length-8 large models on ETTm1 (0.637 versus 0.608) and Electricity (0.150 versus 0.146). Table 11 compares the proposed method’s 64-step forecasts with published 96-step forecasts, so its win count does not establish superiority on the same task.

Significance—the evaluation does not yet establish broad foundation-model advantages. It uses five datasets and one forecast horizon, and Moirai achieves better MSE on three datasets even against the target-calibrated method. Runtime comparisons against competitive patch-based models are absent. Appendix C.4 also shows generated-token compression around 1.4–2.1, substantially below some highlighted input-compression ratios; input compression alone therefore does not establish the claimed generation-efficiency advantage.

Originality and interpretation—the main ingredients are established BPE and empirical conditional-mean estimation. Their combination can be useful, but claims of universally improving forecasting or effectively removing discretization error exceed the evidence. Reconstruction optimality on fitted symbol pairs does not guarantee improved forecasts under distribution shift. Likewise, the weak negative correlations between motif length and error in Table 6 do not establish that longer motifs cause better predictions; smoother, easier segments can produce both longer tokens and lower error.

Reproducibility and limitations: Important details remain unspecified, including inference sampling and point-forecast aggregation, normalization boundaries, handling unseen symbol pairs in conditional decoding, and how forecasts are terminated or truncated with variable-length tokens. Model selection is not clearly separated from test-set reporting. The limitations section focuses on untuned hyperparameters rather than these substantive evaluation restrictions. I identify no material ethical concern, but the unresolved protocol and attribution issues prevent acceptance despite the useful underlying idea.

strengths: Originality and significance: Applying BPE to quantized time series is a useful adaptation that enables variable-length tokens and fewer autoregressive steps. The contribution is practically motivated, even though BPE and conditional-mean estimation are established techniques.

Soundness: The tokenizer is straightforward, and Equation (6) correctly gives the least-squares conditional reconstruction value for observed symbol pairs. Table 13 provides a valuable matched-quantization ablation: motifs improve accuracy over discretization alone on four of five datasets.

Evaluation: The paper explores five model sizes, multiple quantization granularities, vocabulary thresholds, training-data sizes, and synthetic disturbances. Appendix B includes six-seed experiments for selected configurations and end-to-end timing that includes tokenization.
Presentation and reproducibility: The main pipeline is clearly illustrated, and the appendices provide pseudocode, backbone hyperparameters, hardware information, and computational costs.

Research ethics: No material ethical concern is apparent for this general forecasting method. Reporting the substantial training costs is helpful, and the acknowledged lack of backbone hyperparameter tuning is a reasonable limitation.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Section 5.3 fits conditional decoding using each target dataset's training split, and Appendix C.3 explicitly describes fitting it on model predictions. Nevertheless, Tables 2–3 and Figure 9 label the resulting evaluations zero-shot. This is target-specific supervised calibration, so its gains cannot be attributed to a wholly zero-shot pipeline. The source-trained decoder experiment in Table 14 reports improvements relative to quantization error, without establishing comparable end-to-end forecasting gains. These settings need separate reporting and equally calibrated baselines.

Soundness—confounded comparisons: Section 4 gives Chronos and motif models 128 input tokens, which correspond to different amounts of observed history; patch models receive 384 samples. Equal training-token budgets also expose compressed models to more raw samples. These are legitimate operating points for efficiency comparisons, but they do not isolate motif representation as claimed. Matched-history and matched-data-budget experiments are needed. Patch comparisons additionally change the objective from cross-entropy to MSE.

Soundness—headline results and selection: Table 2 combines the best accuracy and fastest qualifying model selected separately across configurations, so the average accuracy improvement and speedup do not describe one operating point. Appendix B reports test-set evaluation without a validation-based selection protocol. Furthermore, the claim that uncalibrated motifs outperform all patch-based Chronos models except on ETTh1 contradicts Table 3: length-8 patches also achieve lower MSE on ETTm1 (0.608 versus 0.637) and Electricity (0.146 versus 0.150).

Soundness—unequal forecasting tasks: Appendix C.2 compares the proposed models' 64-step forecasts against published baseline results for 96-step forecasts, with different contexts, to support the claim of winning 19 of 25 comparisons. Those numbers do not establish superiority on the same task and should be replaced by matched evaluations.

Reproducibility: Important protocol details remain unclear: whether normalization uses only available history, the precise training-corpus exclusions establishing zero-shot status, forecast sampling and aggregation, and handling unseen symbol pairs in conditional decoding. No implementation or checkpoint availability is stated. These omissions matter particularly because the main models are expensive to reproduce.

Significance and interpretation: Five datasets and principally one short forecast horizon provide limited evidence for broad foundation-model generalization. The negative correlations between motif length and prediction error in Table 6 do not establish that longer motifs cause better forecasts; smoother, easier segments can both compress more and incur less error. The limitations discussion should address these evidential boundaries. Overall, the promising tokenizer and extensive ablations do not yet resolve the methodological problems underlying the central performance claims.

strengths: Originality and significance: Applying BPE to quantized time series is a useful, simple approach to variable-length tokenization. It offers an interpretable vocabulary and can reduce autoregressive generation costs without changing the transformer backbone. The contribution lies primarily in this application and its empirical characterization.

Soundness: The basic tokenizer is well specified, and Equation (6) correctly gives the empirical squared-error minimizer for each observed conditioning pair. Results without conditional decoding demonstrate substantial improvements over the sample-based Chronos baseline on several datasets.

Evaluation: The experiments cover five model sizes, three quantization granularities, and multiple forecasting domains. Appendix C.2 includes valuable discretization-only and equal-context-length controls. Additional experiments investigate vocabulary size, noise, transients, and training-data requirements.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline illustrations and pseudocode make the method accessible. Appendix B reports training hyperparameters, hardware, computational costs, and six-seed variability for selected configurations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Tables 2 and 3 describe results including conditional decoding as zero-shot, but Section 5.3 fits that decoder on the respective target dataset's training split using model forecasts. This is supervised target-domain adaptation, even though transformer weights remain frozen. Appendix C.3 acknowledges the distinction, but Table 16 reports improvements relative to quantization error rather than the absolute forecasting MSE needed to establish comparable zero-shot gains. The headline results must clearly separate these protocols.

Soundness—comparative evaluation: Table 13 compares the proposed method's 64-step forecasts against published baselines forecasting 96 steps from 192 context tokens. Consequently, the claim of winning 19 of 25 comparisons does not establish superiority on a matched task. Moreover, the patch-based Chronos comparison changes both tokenization and the objective from cross-entropy to MSE, contradicting the repeated claim that tokenization is the only difference.

Significance—efficiency claims: Table 2 combines the best accuracy and fastest qualifying configuration, often from different model sizes. For Traffic, the approximately 57-fold acceleration compares a large Chronos model with a tiny proposed model; the large-to-large comparison in Table 12 is approximately 2.25-fold. The accuracy–latency tradeoff is useful, but the abstract does not make this distinction clear. Latency comparisons against patch-based models are also missing, leaving the practical efficiency advantage over compressed alternatives unresolved.

Soundness—selection and attribution: Appendix B says results are evaluated and reported on the test set, while Tables 2 and 3 select the best among multiple model sizes and tokenizers separately for each dataset. No independent validation procedure for these selections is described. The appendix controls partially address context length and discretization, but do not jointly control them, and Tables 14 and 15 provide only one ambiguously specified motif configuration against five baseline sizes.

Soundness—conditional decoding: The closed-form optimum is an empirical reconstruction or calibration optimum, not a guarantee of improved forecasting under distribution shift. A decoder conditioned only on the current bin is needed to distinguish benefits of ordinary bin-center recalibration from benefits of conditioning on the previous symbol. Handling unseen conditioning pairs is also unspecified.

Reproducibility: Important details remain unclear, including whether normalization statistics use only observed context, the forecasting sampling or decoding policy and number of sampled trajectories, handling of variable-length generation at the forecast boundary, and training/evaluation dataset-overlap checks. These details materially affect both accuracy and latency. No implementation or checkpoint availability statement is provided.

Presentation and limitations: Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Negative correlations between motif length and error in Table 6 do not establish that longer motifs cause better forecasts; simpler, more predictable regions may produce longer motifs. The limitations discussion focuses on absent hyperparameter tuning and newer backbones, while omitting the restricted 64-step forecasting evaluation, target-data requirements of the strongest decoder results, and weaker results on some datasets. These unresolved evidential issues outweigh the promising tokenizer contribution.

strengths: Originality and significance: Applying BPE to quantized time series provides a useful, simple mechanism for variable-length tokenization. Adaptive compression and fewer autoregressive steps are practically relevant contributions, even though the underlying BPE algorithm is established.

Soundness: The conditional mean in Eq. (6) correctly minimizes the stated empirical squared reconstruction loss for observed symbol pairs. The tokenizer also preserves the underlying quantized sequence while compressing it.

Empirical support: The study covers five model sizes, multiple tokenizers, and diverse datasets. Appendix C.2 includes valuable controls for quantization granularity and input length; these support benefits beyond merely coarsening the bins or extending context, although improvements are not universal.

Presentation and reproducibility: The method is generally understandable, with helpful illustrations, pseudocode, training hyperparameters, hardware and computational costs. Appendix B reports six-seed variability for representative configurations and measures end-to-end inference time, including tokenization.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot and adaptation results are conflated. Tables 2–3 describe comparisons as zero-shot while including conditional decoding trained on each target dataset’s training set using model predictions (Section 5.3). This is supervised target-domain adaptation, even if the backbone remains frozen. Appendix C.3’s data-independent experiment instead measures recovery of quantization error and does not clearly establish corresponding improvements on actual forecast errors. Separate frozen zero-shot forecasting from adapted forecasting and give baselines equivalent adaptation access.

Soundness—the headline accuracy and speed improvements summarize different, retrospectively selected models. Section 5.1 selects the best MSE and, separately, the fastest qualifying model across three tokenizers and five sizes for each dataset. Thus the reported 39.8% MSE improvement and 23.14× acceleration do not describe one deployable configuration achieving both. Appendix B reports test-set evaluation without an independent model-selection protocol. The Pareto plots are useful, but the headline needs qualification and validation-selected configurations.

Comparative evidence has important mismatches. Table 13 supports the claim of winning 19 of 25 comparisons using literature baselines forecasting 96 samples, whereas the proposed models forecast 64. These MSEs do not establish superiority on the same task. Moreover, the patch-based comparison changes both representation and the training objective from cross-entropy to MSE, contradicting the repeated assertion that tokenization is the only difference. Appendix controls help, but do not resolve these issues.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in consequential places. The manuscript does not clearly specify whether normalization statistics use only information available at the forecast origin, how predicted categorical distributions become point forecasts, how unseen conditional-decoding pairs are handled, or how variable-length generation terminates. It also lacks an explicit overlap audit between Chronos pretraining data and evaluation datasets, particularly the Fev-bench subset. These are uncertainties requiring documentation, not evidence that leakage occurred.

Significance and interpretation are overstated relative to the evidence. Evaluation concentrates on a 64-sample horizon and MSE, leaving long-horizon behavior and probabilistic forecast quality unestablished. Table 6’s weak negative correlations between motif length and error do not show that longer motifs cause better predictions: smoother, easier segments can both compress better and incur lower error. Table 3 also shows that the approach is competitive rather than uniformly superior to strong patch-based alternatives.

Originality and limitations need more precise treatment. Conditional decoding is a conditional-mean lookup estimator, and motif discovery directly applies established BPE; the strongest novelty is their time-series application and empirical characterization. Claims such as universally improving forecasting or effectively removing discretization error exceed what is proved. The limitations discussion acknowledges computational constraints but omits the more consequential adaptation, selection, and evaluation restrictions above. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the rejection is driven by evidential weaknesses in central claims.

strengths: Originality: Applying BPE to quantized time series provides a useful, simple mechanism for variable-length tokenization. The contribution includes empirical understanding of how quantization, motif frequency, and vocabulary size affect compression and forecasting.

Soundness: The tokenizer is clearly specified, and the conditional-mean decoder correctly minimizes the stated empirical squared-error objective for observed symbol pairs. Appendix C.2 includes valuable quantization-only and matched-context comparisons, supporting benefits beyond simply supplying longer histories.

Significance: Forecasting improvements without conditional decoding are substantial on several datasets. Adaptive compression and fewer autoregressive steps offer a practical route to reducing inference cost with standard transformer architectures.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides pseudocode, training hyperparameters, hardware and computational costs, full model-size results, and six-seed experiments for selected configurations. The vocabulary, robustness, and embedding analyses provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: Soundness—zero-shot claims: Tables 2 and 3 label conditional-decoding results as zero-shot, but Section 5.3 fits the decoder on model predictions and targets from each evaluation dataset’s training split. This is supervised target-domain adaptation, even without backbone fine-tuning. Appendix C.3 reports source-trained decoding gains relative to quantization error rather than clearly reporting absolute forecasting MSE under the same protocol. The main comparisons need to separate these settings and give baselines equivalent adaptation opportunities.

Soundness—headline efficiency: The 23.14× acceleration and 39.8% MSE improvement describe separately selected operating points, not one configuration achieving both. The fastest qualifying model and best-MSE model are selected separately for each test dataset across tokenizers and sizes. These are useful retrospective frontier comparisons, but do not establish a deployable selection rule or a same-size tokenization speedup. Table 12 shows much smaller same-size accelerations, and Weather’s no-decoding acceleration in Table 2 is only 0.26×.

Soundness—comparison controls: The patch baseline changes both tokenization and the loss from cross-entropy to MSE, contradicting the claim that tokenization is the only difference. Equal training-token budgets also expose compressed models to more underlying observations. Additionally, Table 13 compares the proposed 64-step forecasts against published 96-step forecasts with different contexts, so the claim of winning 19 of 25 comparisons is not supported by a matched evaluation.

Reproducibility: Important forecasting details remain unspecified, including the normalization window, token sampling or selection procedure, conversion of categorical forecasts into point estimates, handling of unseen decoder symbol pairs, and stopping or truncation of variable-length generated motifs. The manuscript also does not clearly document pretraining/evaluation overlap checks for its selected FEV datasets. These omissions materially impede reproducing and interpreting the zero-shot results.

Originality and interpretation: Conditional decoding is a straightforward conditional-mean lookup estimator; its novelty lies mainly in its application here. No unconditioned learned-bin decoder or simple calibration baseline establishes how much improvement specifically requires the previous symbol. Likewise, negative correlations between motif length and error do not establish that longer motifs cause better forecasts: simpler, more predictable segments may naturally receive longer tokens.

Significance and limitations: Evaluation uses a single 64-sample horizon, and the main efficiency evidence centers on sample-wise Chronos rather than strong patch-based alternatives. The acknowledged lack of hyperparameter tuning is reasonable, but the limitations discussion should also address these scope restrictions and target-domain decoder fitting. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the decisive concern is that useful tokenizer results are accompanied by central claims whose evaluation protocols do not yet adequately support them.
